title: Printing Messages
story: Imagine you're making a sign for a party. You want to write several lines — 'Welcome!', the date, the time, and maybe a fun message. Your program can do the same thing: print one line, then another, then another, building up a full display piece by piece.
why: Real programs don't just do one thing — they do many things in order. Learning to print multiple messages teaches you how the computer reads your code from top to bottom.
analogy: A program reads top-to-bottom, like reading a page in a book — you start at the first line and work your way down.
try_it: Add a line that prints your age as a number. Then add another line that prints your age with quotes around it — what's different? Now add one more line that prints your shoe size as a number.
tips: Text goes inside double quotes `"..."`. Numbers do NOT need quotes — just write them as they are.
The computer runs your instructions in the exact order you write them, top to bottom.
Each `io.println` call starts a new line — three calls gives you three lines of output.
Mixing text and numbers in your output makes your program feel like a real conversation.
common_mistakes: Putting quotes around numbers: `io.println("42")` treats 42 as text, not a number. Use `io.println("42")` for actual numbers.
Forgetting to add a second `io.println` call — remember, every message needs its own instruction.
Writing multiple messages inside one `io.println` separated by commas — XIOM prints only one thing per call.
Forgetting the semicolon `;` at the end of any `io.println` line.
